newsitem.title: UK: IEA says not in favour of German oil sale proposal.
newsitem.headline: IEA says not in favour of German oil sale proposal.

text.p: The International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday it was not in favour of Germany's proposal to sell part of the nation's emergency oil stockpile but that German oil stocks would still meet legal requirements.
"The IEA would consider this unfortunate but even if they do sell these stocks Germany would still meet the IEA requirement of 90 days forward cover," said an IEA spokesman in Paris.
Bonn on Thursday said it was thinking of selling 7.3 million tonnes of crude, about 20 percent of total strategic reserves, to help plug holes in government finances.
The oil involved, the entire federal crude reserve, has been stored since 1975 in salt caverns near the northern port of Wilhelmshaven.
A decision on whether the sale will proceed is expected by July 11.
Germany is searching for ways to cut its budget deficit this year and next to meet the strict borrowing requirements for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
The IEA said the sale would be of a "significant" proportion, reducing German stocks by about 25 days of forward cover to 95 days.

Under emergency reserve obligations signed in 1975, IEA members are required to hold at least 90 days of net imports and release oil in the event of serious market turmoil. The IEA has used the weapon once, at the start of the Gulf War in January 1991.

The agency, made up of members of the Organisation for Cooperation and Development (OECD), was set up in 1974 in the wake of an oil price shock to protect the industrialised nations against further price rises.
OECD countries rely on imported oil, including big flows from the Middle East, to cover just over half their needs.
Germany's proposal comes within weeks of a meeting of IEA energy ministers in Paris.
The IEA warned member countries against complacency in protecting energy security which it said remained its top priority.
The warning followed controversy over recent sales of U.S. government stocks and a decline in stocks held by private oil companies in an effort to economise.
The IEA has criticised the sales from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve at a time when America's imports are rising.
U.S. Energy Secretary Federico Pena has pledged to reverse a decision to further reduce U.S. oil stocks in 2002.
